newsitem.title: UK: London's City says EMU not supported by economic case.
newsitem.headline: London's City says EMU not supported by economic case.

text.p: Political will for European Economic and Monetary Union (EMU) is not backed up by a convincing economic and business case, representatives of London's financial centre said on Tuesday.

Of around 250 business people taking part in a City Debate, 58 percent voted against a motion stating that "a powerful business and economic case" underpinned the political momentum towards forming a single currency.
While four percent of those present abstained, 38 percent voted in favour of the motion.

"It is conceivable that Europe is heading for an economic disaster by forming a single currency," said Anatole Kaletsky, the economics editor of Britain's Times newspaper, speaking against the motion.
"That is certainly not an argument for the UK to join them."

Also speaking for the opposition, Tim Melville-Ross, director general of the Institute of Directors, said different cultures, different economic cycles, different legal systems and different educational standards within Europe meant there was no economic or business case for EMU.

He said convergence criteria laid down in the Maastricht Treaty did not go far enough and would still leave too many fundamental discrepancies between the economies of countries wishing to start a single currency in January 1999.
"For a single currency to have the remotest prospect of working without creating enormous economic damage, a far greater degree of convergence is required," he said.

But Peter Sutherland, chairman of Goldman Sachs International, said the benefits of a single currency -- increased economic growth, lower inflation, increased trade and a more cohesive European Union -- far outweighed the cost to a nation of giving up its monetary sovereignty.
"The economic arguments for EMU are as strong as the political ones," said Sutherland. "The single market cannot long survive if currencies fluctuate."
Jan Timmer, member of the supervisory board of the electronics firm Philips, also said loss of sovereignty in economic policy was an argument that did not hold water.
"In a world where we talk of globalisation, deregulation and other things designed to advance economic progress, economic sovereignty is a myth," he told the debate.
Timmer called for strong leadership from European governments, saying that the euro was a must if Europe was to head off increasing competition from the U.S. and Japan.
"To hesitate now would be an opportunity lost forever," he said.
